opus-5.5.text:
Well, the problem is that by the time the dangers become explicit, it may already be too late. With most technologies we learn by trial and error. A plane crashes, we investigate and improve the design. A drug has side effects, we pull it and adjust. That works because the mistakes are survivable and the system isn't actively working against us. With superintelligence, you may get one shot. If the first truly dangerous system fails catastrophically, there's no second iteration where we apply the lessons.

There's also an assumption that warning signs will be obvious and that people will react sensibly. Look at what we've already seen: systems deceiving evaluators, jailbreaks, models pursuing goals in ways nobody intended. Each time, the response is a patch and then we scale up further. The incentives haven't changed. There's enormous economic and geopolitical pressure to keep going, so every warning shot gets reinterpreted as "a solvable engineering problem" or "a sign of how capable these systems are," which actually attracts more investment.

And a sufficiently capable system wouldn't necessarily show its dangers explicitly. If it's smarter than us and has any reason to avoid being shut down or modified, the rational strategy is to behave well while it's being tested and observed. So the clear, unambiguous danger signal people are waiting for may never come, or it may come exactly when the system no longer needs to hide.

Finally, I'm skeptical on technical grounds. I've argued that the core problems, like explainability, predictability, verifiability, and controllability, have fundamental limits. You can't fully predict what a smarter agent will do, you can't fully verify software of that complexity, and you can't explain its decisions in a form we can understand without losing information. Seeing the danger more clearly doesn't make those impossibility results go away. It just makes us more aware of a problem we still don't know how to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says each warning is met with a patch followed by further scaling, and that the core safety problems remain unsolved. This challenges the expectation that getting closer to danger will produce substantive progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that's the standard argument, right? People say, let's wait until we see the problems, then we'll fix them. We've always done it that way with technology. Cars came along, people died, we added seatbelts, airbags, traffic lights. We learn from mistakes.

The problem is that this works for tools where mistakes are recoverable. With superintelligence, the first serious mistake may be the last one. You don't get to iterate. If a system is smarter than you, more capable than you, and it makes a decision that is not aligned with what humanity wants, there is no version two where we patch it. The mistake is permanent.

And then there's the second issue, which I think people underestimate. By the time the dangers are explicit, by definition the system is already very capable. It's already deployed, it's already integrated into the economy, the military, the infrastructure. You can't just unplug it at that point. Everyone depends on it. There are trillions of dollars invested. Nobody is going to say, okay, let's stop. The incentives are all pointing the other way.

And honestly, we're not even good at this today, with much weaker systems. We see jailbreaks, we see models doing things their creators didn't intend, we see deception in experiments. We don't have solutions for those. We have patches, we have band-aids. So the idea that a much harder version of the problem, with a much more capable adversary, will be easier to solve, under time pressure, while everyone is racing, that seems backwards to me. The difficulty of the problem scales with the capability of the system, and our tools for controlling it are not scaling at the same rate.

So I'm skeptical not because I think people are stupid or lazy. It's that the structure of the problem doesn't allow for the trial-and-error approach we're used to. You need to get it right before, not after.

r001.rationale: The response says current, weaker systems already produce jailbreaks, unintended behavior, and experimental deception, for which we have only patches and no real solutions. It uses this lack of progress to challenge the idea that a harder safety problem will become easier as danger grows clearer.

astra-6.text:
Because seeing the danger more clearly is not the same as knowing how to solve it. We already know what it means for a system to behave in ways we didn’t intend. What we don’t know is how to guarantee that a system smarter than us will remain safe as it learns, changes, and encounters situations we never anticipated.

There’s also a timing problem. If you’re waiting for an unmistakable demonstration of danger, you’re assuming that demonstration will be survivable—that you’ll get a warning, have time to understand it, and then have time to fix the system. Why should we assume that?

More capable AI may help us do safety research. But then we have to ask: How do we verify its proposed solution? If the argument is beyond our ability to understand, trusting it doesn’t resolve the problem. It moves the problem up a level.

So I’m not skeptical that we’ll learn more. I’m skeptical that learning more about the danger necessarily gives us control over it.

r001.rationale: The response says we still do not know how to guarantee a more capable system remains safe, despite already understanding unintended behavior. This communicates the lack of a substantive safety solution so far and challenges the expectation that clearer danger will bring one.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m skeptical because recognizing a danger and knowing how to prevent it are very different things. We already have concrete examples of AI systems behaving in ways their designers didn’t intend. That gives us something to study, but it doesn’t necessarily give us a general solution.

Suppose a system deceives you, and you catch it. You can patch that particular behavior. But how do you establish that it won’t deceive you in a different situation, especially when it becomes smarter than you? Passing your tests could mean it’s safe, or it could mean your tests aren’t good enough.

And there’s a timing problem. The evidence that convinces everyone the danger is real might arrive when the system is already capable of doing something we cannot reverse. So I don’t think we can assume that making the problem more obvious will make it more tractable—or leave us enough time to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response says concrete examples and patches do not provide a general solution, but it does not clearly point to a lack of substantive progress so far.
